cells.tense: Standing at the bench, the whole pattern visible, and the hand still on the tool.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you've built slowly and write down what it taught you that the fast version couldn't. Leave it where you'll run into it again. Keeping what the long work showed you is the next pass.
cells.core:
You can look at the whole shape of something and still keep working the same piece past the point of quickness — most days you do, and each pass shows you something the last one didn't. That's not stubbornness. That's how a craft gets into your hands, and it's why the things you make tend to be right the first time out in the world.

The next thing this can feed isn't more hours at the bench. It's keeping what the slow passes have shown you on purpose — writing it down, saying it out loud, letting it shape the next piece rather than only the last one. You're free to want the sharper version, not just the finished one.
cells.sheetLine: The long work is showing you what quick work couldn't.
cells.verb: Building one thing past the point of quickness, each pass finer than the last, until the making itself becomes the knowledge.
cells.place: The room where the whole shape of something can be seen at once without stepping out of it.

cells.tense: Still adding passes for a moment that hasn't arrived, building past where anyone asked.
cells.ask: Take one finished thing to people who care about the same thing and let it be done in front of them. Say what it is and stop. What the room gives back is the next material.
cells.core:
On a good day you finish the piece, you hand it over, and you watch it get used by someone else — that's the moment the work stops being yours alone and starts being something. It lands, and you move on to the next thing with the bench clear.

Right now each new pass is meant to be the one that finishes it, and none of them do, because the finishing isn't at the bench anymore. The work only completes when it reaches other people, and until it does the standard keeps sliding away from you, one more revision out of reach.

cells.tense: Past the door of the long work, still standing at a threshold you already crossed.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you've been circling and say it plainly to one person — what it is, what you see, what you'd build. Out loud, today, without the caveats. The shape wants to be declared, not just held.
cells.core:
When the long work is running well, you can walk someone through a whole thing in one sitting and they leave knowing what to do next — you do that easily, and it comes from the same hands on the same material over time, pass after pass, until the shape of it is just there when you look. Handing someone that whole view is what the practice was for.

Lately the long passes aren't happening. The days fill with smaller things that don't leave you anything sharper, and the place where the whole pattern used to be obvious feels quiet. You keep walking past the bench and calling that being practical.

cells.tense: Already reading the whole shape and calling it something that arrived on its own.
cells.ask: Name one pattern you spotted before anyone else — what it was, what it meant, what you did with it — and say plainly that you're the one who saw it. To one person, in your own words. Put your name on it.
cells.core:
You're already reading the shape of things before most people have noticed the parts. In meetings, in conversations, you know where something is going, and later you mention it as if it had just shown up on its own. That read works — it's useful, it's usually right, and people rely on you for it.

What's missing is saying it's yours. The read runs on what moves in you when you look, not on what the room handed you, and calling it the data, or the obvious, borrows against the one person who actually did the reading. The work you've done belongs on the sentence.
